title: Solar eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
description: At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves."I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not b
body: At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves."I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders."I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme."People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.How and when to see the solar eclipseWith around 90% of the Sun set to be obscured by the Moon, the UK is expecting its most significant eclipse in 27 years.The right glasses should have the international safety standard ISO 12312-2 printed on them, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has advised, and the lenses should not be scratched, torn or damaged.It has also advised caution surrounding glasses being sold online, as the scramble for safe spectacles has prompted eclipse chasers to trawl social media for tips.Even just a small part of the Sun breaking through the glasses can harm your eyes, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists has warned, adding that the safest way to watch the event is indirectly - such as through a livestream or broadcast."Crucially, the retina has no pain receptors, so people will not feel the damage as it happens," explains the college's president Mohamed Elalfy.The college reported around 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching 1999's total solar eclipse - around 40% of those affected had looked at it for less than a minute.Anyone who notices a change in their vision after looking at the Sun should seek advice from an eye-care professional.Imo Bell, a planetarium astronomer at The Royal Observatory Greenwich, says the specialist glasses are "very, very different" to regular sunglasses, which will not offer protection."They block out so much light that you can't see anything through them except the Sun," she told the PA news agency.The UKHSA explains that regular sunglasses can also reduce glare and make it more comfortable for you to look at the Sun for longer - causing more damage.You should not use binoculars, telescopes or the viewfinder of a camera even with your eclipse glasses on, because their magnifying effect can nullify the protection of the glasses and damage your sight.For those without glasses or wanting to watch directly, you can do so using a pinhole projector.You can make a simple one with a single sheet of card or something more ambitious using a cardboard box."We're not going to get one this good for a really long time," says Bell. "So, it's important not to miss it, and to be prepared."

schema.headline: Solar eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low

title: Anne Hathaway pokes fun at 'fake baby bump' theories
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Anne Hathaway put her bump on full show in a custom Atelier Prabal Gurung crop topByIan YoungsCulture reporterAnne Hat
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Anne Hathaway put her bump on full show in a custom Atelier Prabal Gurung crop topByIan YoungsCulture reporterAnne Hathaway has poked fun at those who suggested her baby bump didn't look real after a recent film premiere, telling them she had "fake hair, real bump".The US actress turned heads in an outfit that showed off her bare bump at the launch of her new film, The End of Oak Street, in Los Angeles on Sunday.It sparked a flurry of comments on social media, external from people saying "Why does it look fake?" and "Oh come on. That is not real." But others leapt to her defence, with one writing: "A lot of people in these comments have never seen a pregnant belly on someone who has abs."Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she is expecting her third child with husband Adam Shulman.Letting it all hang outHer growing bump has been evident as she has promoted The Odyssey in recent weeks, but it attracted greater attention thanks to her choice of outfit at the premiere for The End of Oak Street.The bump was on full show in the custom Atelier Prabal Gurung crop top, which the designer described as a "sculptural high-low halter top with a cascading train". Hathaway paired the top with low-rise La Ligne jeans and red Aquazzura stilettos.Image source, EPA"Fake hair, real bump," the actress wrote on Instagram, external with a video of her getting ready and attending the premiere."Enjoy The @endofoakstreet Block Party chaos with me as my outfit literally melts in the heat!!"As well as raising unfounded doubts about the bump, some people criticised the star's overall look on social media, calling it "ridiculous", "tacky" and "bizarre".But others praised her. Charlotte Cripps wrote in the Independent, external: "It might be an outfit that her social media critics wouldn't be seen dead in, but it's a clear message of body positivity, strength, and gender equality – and it's her unique expression of the next chapter of her life."The Telegraph's Rebecca Cope said, external: "Though drawing criticism from some, the look is just the latest example of a celebrity literally letting it all hang out."Hathaway's appearance on Sunday also led to a surge in interest in her "coconut water" nails look, external.Anne Hathaway's bump on the red carpetThe star has been in the spotlight throughout the summer, promoting The Odyssey at its premiere in London on 6 July (below).Image source, ReutersShe also donned red carpet maternity wear at The Odyssey's US premiere in New York on 14 July.Image source, Getty Images

schema.headline: Anne Hathaway pokes fun at 'fake baby bump' theories

title: Jewish headteachers 'spend more time on security than teaching'
description: Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBCImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Antisemitism in schools reached t
body: Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBCImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Antisemitism in schools reached the highest level ever recorded this yearHeadteachers of some Jewish schools are spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than on educational matters, a review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has found.Sir David Bell, speaking for the first time about his ongoing government-commissioned independent review, told the BBC he had been struck by how many leaders of Jewish faith schools had told him security was their main concern - and that "sometimes education takes second place to that".The extent of antisemitism directed at children and young people was "shocking" he said.The report, due ithis autumn, examines experiences of Jewish pupils and staff in faith and secular schools and colleges in England. Sir David said he found that pupils were "subject to regular harassment and abuse".He said Jewish children and young people "are facing a pressure - and indeed one might say even a crisis - that is not the experience of other communities in this country".The review is likely to recommend dedicated training for all teachers and improved education about antisemitism for pupils, the BBC has been told.The BBC has spoken to several headteachers and staff at Jewish schools. All asked not to be named because of concerns over their security and that of their schools.One headteacher said: "In recent years [security] has become an overwhelming priority and increased a significant amount. There have been weeks where approximately 90% of my time has been spent on security-related matters."Security concerns can become one of the many things that headteachers carry with them beyond the school day and, quite literally, can be among the things that keep me awake at night."Image source, University of SunderlandImage caption, Sir David Bell said it was "quite shocking" to see how many young people had encountered antisemitismAnother headteacher, who has led a different Jewish school for 13 years, told the BBC: "I've never spent so much of my time and so much energy dealing with security issues, talking to governors and parents, and above all making daily decisions about how to ensure children in our school are safe."He said it prevented him from "working on educational priorities and on improving our school - instead my focus and time has been spent on security, something that should be a given for every child in this country".Sir David Bell, a former Ofsted chief inspector and senior civil servant at the Department for Education, is now vice-chancellor of the University of Sunderland.  He has heard evidence from pupils, teachers, governors and parents across both the state and independent sectors as well as community organisations.The Bell review has also drawn evidence from a bespoke survey of 5,000 children conducted by the universities, colleges, and admissions service, Ucas. It found about 20% had experienced or observed antisemitic behaviour in schools and colleges.Sir David said: "When you think about antisemitism, you assume that it's going to be directed towards adults… What's been quite shocking is the extent to which antisemitism is encountered by children and young people."'Nazi salutes became quite widespread'Recent figures from the Community Security Trust, an organisation which provides security for the Jewish community, showed a spike in antisemitic incidents at schools.It found in the first half of 2026, antisemitism in schools reached the highest level ever recorded for the first six months of any year. It jumped by 59%, from 112 reported incidents in the first half of 2025, to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.Dr Dave Rich, director of policy at the CST,  said the review was timely and hopes "it will lead to practical recommendations that help educational institutions tackle antisemitism effectively."Education Secretary Lucy Powell told the BBC the review was a "vital piece of work" and she would "carefully consider the conclusions and recommendations to ensure we do what is necessary to prevent antisemitism in our schools and colleges".She said in a statement: "Antisemitism has no place in our society, let alone our education system. Jewish children and staff should never face hatred or prejudice, and every school and college must be equipped to tackle it when it happens."One teenager who gave evidence to the Bell review is Jonathan Frisher, from Cheshire. Now a sixth former, Jonathan was the only Jewish student at his school. He first experienced antisemitic bullying when he started secondary school in 2020."Having one single lesson about modern-day antisemitism really did help," he said."Attitudes changed immediately and people did apologise to me. I experienced a lot less antisemitism. If it works in my school, there's no reason that it can't work in every school across the country."Image caption, Jonathan Frisher: "People were telling me that I should be in a gas chamber"Sir David said the majority of the 700 people who had responded directly to his "call for evidence" were Jewish parents and pupils at non-faith schools.He said the evidence has led him to realise that many schools do not record antisemitic abuse in part because of a lack of understanding about how to recognise it.When his report is published, he is likely to recommend a standardised approach to reporting and recording antisemitic incidents in schools and colleges.Jonathan Frisher's own experiences have led him to campaign for antisemitism education to be made compulsory in schools. A petition he started has gained nearly 40,000 signatures.He said: "People were telling me that I should be in a gas chamber. Swastikas were drawn in lots of classrooms and Nazi salutes became quite widespread. Obviously for someone whose family suffered in the Holocaust it was incredibly difficult to have to deal with comments like that."'My car is searched with an under-car mirror'Sir David added that pupils travelling to and from Jewish schools were "subject to regular harassment and abuse". Pupils aged 12 and 13 in one Jewish faith school in London told him they were regularly abused on the school journey and on public transport. "It's a very different experience for these children and young people to what the vast majority of children and young people in this country face when they're going to and from school and college," he said.He said many teachers at Jewish faith schools reported that going out on school trips was more hazardous than before.One teacher at a Jewish primary school told the BBC security had been stepped up since the spate of arson attacks against Jewish sites and the stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green earlier this year.She said: "There's a security presence patrolling outside the school, inside the school, at all times of day. When I get to school in the morning and enter the car park, my car is searched with an under-car mirror."She added that recent incidents had at times contributed to a "heavy" atmosphere.She said: "There have been reports from parents that antisemitic comments have been made while [pupils] are walking to school. We've had children at music events and sporting events who were booed. There was a comment made about big noses at one of the events that we took the children to."We do what we can to shield the children from a lot of it, but also, if they approach me with their concerns, I can't ignore it. And when one of my pupils said to me, 'Why do people hate Jews so much?', that was really difficult for me to answer."It just goes to show what they're internalising."Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Jewish headteachers 'spend more time on security than teaching'

title: 'I won Commonwealth Games bronze - then went back to work at McDonald's'
description: Shaw won Scotland's first judo medal at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, a bronze in the 48kg event."It's so cool when it's something you've
body: Shaw won Scotland's first judo medal at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, a bronze in the 48kg event."It's so cool when it's something you've dreamed of doing since you were eight years old - and suddenly you're there," Shaw told BBC Sport."To get there was crazy, and to come away with a medal was even better."Shaw won that medal on the last Friday of the Games. The next week, she was back at the family home in Surrey - and back to work."I picked up that part-time job [at McDonald's] when I was studying for my A-levels," said Shaw, who qualifies to represent Scotland through her father's side of the family.She has recently been based largely in Birmingham while studying for a biology degree. That means she has been close to the British Judo Olympic and Paralympic National Training Centre in Walsall."They've been really flexible with me, letting me work when I can. They've been really good with me," she said."It's mostly seasonal because my job's back at home, but when I am back it is like two, three shifts a week."It's hard to find jobs like it though that are flexible with your hours. I've heard from other people in their part-time jobs saying their boss won't give them the weekend off."Shaw is a world-class competitor in a sport where the rewards may not make her wealthy."Obviously there's football, Formula One… but I can't think of many more sports where it is a case of 'you've hit the top level and now you're financially settled'," she said.Shaw is given what is called an 'Athlete Performance Award' (APA), a financial grant from UK Sport and the National Lottery that contributes towards her living and training costs.There are different grades of support, external that athletes receive, depending on their results and prospect of medal-winning performances.Shaw told BBC Sport that it was "very common" for athletes in sports like judo to have another source of income."The money I get [APA] covers my living expenses, which is a blessing and not to be taken for granted," she said."But, for example, the next competition I've paid for myself because it wasn't funded by British Judo."Going to Peru [for the Grand Prix] has cost me quite a bit of money and then I'm not really getting that back from anywhere else."I'm also a normal person! Like, I want to save for a house."Athletes can also earn money through sponsorships, something Shaw says would be a "game-changer" for an athlete at the present stage of her career."It just means you can take every single opportunity… put it towards competitions that I don't get funded."Shaw also decided to set up a GoFundMe page at the start of the year, which she sees as a way of helping to fund her dream of going to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

schema.headline: 'I won Commonwealth Games bronze - then went back to work at McDonald's'

title: Gianni Infantino: Division over Fifa president shown in map of support and opposition
description: As recently as mid-July, Gianni Infantino was considered a shoo-in to be re-elected as Fifa president next March.All but a handful of Fifa's 210 membe
body: As recently as mid-July, Gianni Infantino was considered a shoo-in to be re-elected as Fifa president next March.All but a handful of Fifa's 210 members had endorsed his bid for a fourth term in charge of world football, and he faced no meaningful challenge from any quarter.But that picture looks very different now, after two weeks of relentless fallout to his now-abandoned plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors.The world is far from united over whether Infantino should stay or go.To illustrate that division, BBC Sport has mapped the apparent view of all 210 member associations who are able to vote (Nepal, Fifa's 211th member, is currently suspended and has no voting rights).In some cases, countries have publicly stated their overt support or opposition regarding Infantino.Others have directly told BBC Sport where they stand when asked to do so, while some are assumed positions based on statements made by the continental confederation the country sits within.Whereas once Infantino looked set to saunter to a fourth term unopposed, he now might need to have enough numbers on his side to stay in post.If a unity candidate is found to oppose him, then the election would become a direct battle.Fifa election votes between two candidates require a simple majority - each candidate would require a total of 106 votes to win.If there are three or more candidates, a first-round win requires two thirds of the vote. If there is no winner, there is a second round where a simple majority is needed.Europe has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, North America 35, Oceania 11 and South America 10.But while the current tally looks like 73 in support of Infantino, 124 in opposition to him and 13 undecided, that picture is fluid and is likely to change in the months ahead.Several European countries, including England and Wales, have formally withdrawn letters of support for Infantino that they had sent for next year's election.On Monday, the backlash against Infantino intensified when European governing body Uefa, North America's Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) signed a joint letter accusing him and Fifa of breaking their trust "through deception".It is a significant coalition, and those regional governing bodies represent 136 associations between them.But there are already dissenting members within the confederations, like Bhutan, the Philippines, and the UAE within Asia, who have all backed Infantino.Indeed, Asia is considered a potential swing region for Infantino's future, with many associations not yet making their position known.Mexico has broken ranks within Concacaf by coming out in support of Infantino, too. The USA and Canada have stated support for Concacaf's latest statement, but have not outright declared their opposition to Infantino's rule.And the Oceania Football Confederation (OFC) has made no public comment since the whole saga began - nor have any of its members. OFC told BBC Sport they will release a statement following a meeting on Thursday.Infantino still has staunch allies too, particularly within Africa (Caf) and South America (Conmebol), who have benefited from unprecedented investment since he took over a decade ago.That investment could help him gain critical votes from nations within AFC, Concacaf and OFC - who are lower down the football food chain and have benefited significantly from the Fifa Forward programme, which has made billions of dollars available for investment.And Saudi Arabia - which has yet to take a public position but was awarded hosting rights for the 2034 World Cup on Infantino's watch - will have its own football leadership elections in August. The results could dictate the kingdom's position, and influence the view of others in the region.It cannot be guaranteed that every nation will toe the line of their confederation.Infantino has shown no desire to step down, but there is a chance that his time in charge could be over by the autumn.That could come to pass if Fifa Council members try to force his resignation at an emergency meeting.Such a meeting can be called, and must take place within a fortnight, if 19 of the 37 members call for it.The council is made up of nine members from Uefa, seven from AFC, six from Caf, five from Concacaf, five from Conmebol, and three from Oceania. Also on the panel are Infantino himself and Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.Given its makeup, then, this approach is probably unlikely.Which leaves the possibility of a candidate standing against Infantino next March. Nobody has put their name forward yet, but if the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf, and AFC are serious about toppling Infantino, uniting behind a single candidate is likely their best option.The deadline for a candidate to announce their intention to stand is November.Historically, other confederations have been angered by European dominance of football, its competitions and its wealth.That is perhaps why Concacaf president Victor Montagliani has been consistently mooted as the most likely challenger to Infantino in recent weeks.The map of votes could change significantly based on who stands.If AFC president Sheikh Salman were to step forward, for example, there is a chance that could sway some of the associations in Asia that are currently supportive of Infantino towards him.For now, the global picture remains unclear because of emerging splits within confederations, the potential for key players to declare one way or another in the coming months and the hitherto lack of a clear candidate to challenge Infantino.What is clear is that Infantino is no longer coasting towards a fourth term, if he clings on that long.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Division over Fifa president shown in map of support and opposition

title: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides
description: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhua
body: Figure caption, Watch: Chinese man targeted by 'flash wedding' scamsByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing and GuiyangAt 37, Wang Zhuang had almost given up hope of finding a wife, until he saw the glossy matchmaking adverts.They promised he wouldn't have to waste years on building a relationship that had no future. They offered to introduce him to a demure, devoted woman."The matchmakers said that girls from Guizhou are frugal," Wang says. "They told me they are good at running a household, able to do housework, and their families are very poor, so after marrying into your family, they would settle down and live a life with you."So Wang travelled to Guiyang, a city in the southwestern province of Guizhou, in the hope of finding his soulmate.He thought he had, when he was matched with a woman who seemed to tick every box. They had only met a few times before they married.Then, almost as quickly as his new life had begun, it was over."My whole family has been thrown into chaos," he says, shaking his head.He is still picking up the pieces more than a year after he discovered that everything he had been told by his wife was a lie.She was a former karaoke hostess who'd been married three times, had three children, a serious sexually transmitted disease and was deeply in debt. She had even lied about her age.He is fighting for a divorce and cannot return home to his old life - at least until he can recoup some of his life savings, which he says he paid to the agency within hours of being introduced to several potential matches."My parents blame me. I have insomnia and anxiety. I can't focus on work."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chinese brides are in huge demand because of a steep gender imbalanceWang's story is an extreme symptom of a demographic crisis that has long been in the making in China.For decades, China's Communist Party decreed that couples could have only one child. They reversed course in January 2016 but by then the "one-child" policy, coupled with a preference for boys, had produced a shrinking pool of women and a stark gender imbalance.There are now 30 million more men than women in China – that's more than the male population of the UK, or the entire population of Australia.This has left men like Wang, who are in their late 30s and who live in smaller cities or far-flung, rural areas, with few options. Women in these places can afford to be choosy as they know they are in demand."The requirements for men are very high in my city. You need to have a car, a house and your family should preferably run a business," he says.Many families also demand a high "bride price", a longstanding Chinese custom where the groom's family gives money to the bride. In parts of China, where men far outnumber women, this has become a significant financial burden.Hence the appeal of matchmaking agencies like the ones in Guizhou, which are proposing a one-stop, quick solution - or "flash marriages".Matchmaking agencies are hardly new in China, but many seem to be finding vulnerable targets in men who are struggling to find partners as they grow older.So much so that state media recently reported that the industry had seen "rapid growth" which  had "bred illegal practices and chaos".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The "flash marriage" market is now on Beijing's radarIt's hard to determine the scale of such fraud across China but it has grown enough to draw the attention of Chinese officials. Between January 2024 and March 2025, prosecutors handled cases involving 1,546 individuals for crimes related to the matchmaking industry.This month, five separate authorities jointly launched a nationwide crackdown on the matchmaking industry after the issue generated "widespread public concern".In one case, a matchmaking agency reportedly used karaoke waitresses as bait to defraud 128 victims of more than 2.5 million yuan (£274,000, $371,000)."I think the government could introduce industry-specific regulations targeting flash marriage scams," Fan Binghe, from the Nanjing Office of the Beijing Jingshi law firm, told the BBC.Although Guiyang has become synonymous with this booming "flash marriage" market, there is little to suggest it is a romantic hub.The agency offices sit in a dense warren of buildings above a shopping precinct, where vendors sell local fruit and workers queue for takeaway sour soup rice noodles.Wang, however, was convinced he could trust them after the company told him they would do a full background check and that he would be entitled to compensation if he was the victim of fraud.So he paid up and the introductions began.Image caption, Wang was drawn to Guiyang by the promise of a demure spouse He met seven women in various "blind date" rooms over a few days while being carefully supervised by agency staff. He asked questions about where they came from, if they'd been married before and if they had any kids.He set his heart on the eighth woman he met. He was hoping to meet someone who hadn't been married before, with no children and who was just a little younger than him."She also dressed very simply," he recalls. "She looked introverted and honest."They met four or five times for just eight to 10 minutes each time. He says they had been under strict instructions not to exchange phone numbers or any details on private messages, or they would be fined.After two or three days he decided she was the one and he agreed to pay her a substantial bride price. "I spent more than 300,000 yuan [$44,000]," he says, with a pile of well-thumbed legal papers in hand to prove it."If you include the wedding banquet and everything else, I spent around 400,000 to 500,000 yuan."The whole process was documented by the matchmaking agency in a series of glossy photos, which they also use to advertise their services on Chinese social media. In the video the couple are holding hands on a red carpet and smiling while romantic music plays in the background.Image caption, Wang with his ex-wife in a photo taken soon after their wedding  Just months into the marriage, debt collectors started calling, alleging she owed them money.Wang grew suspicious and wanted to know what else she had kept hidden. He checked her phone and found details of her former life, her birth certificate and former marriage documents.When he confronted her, she offered him a divorce, but refused to return a single penny of the bride price.He says he tried to hunt down the agency responsible for his marriage, but when he returned to their offices, they had packed up and disappeared.From his rented flat in Guiyang, just across from the main district which houses most of these agencies, Wang now spends his time making social media videos trying to warn other men about what can go wrong.In Guiyang, it is difficult to find an agency where the staff is willing to talk. One agency boss agreed to talk to us in their offices – although his business partner later asked us to leave.Inside there was a red carpet littered with fake petals ready for a proposal. He told us a couple had pledged to marry just hours before we arrived."There's a huge market for flash marriages in China. It only really emerged over the last two or three years," he told us.The agencies claim families here did not strictly adhere to the one-child policy, which means the area has a larger pool of women. "Even if a family had two or three daughters, they would keep trying for a son," one of them told the BBC.They say they are now trying to match these women with men from central provinces – like Wang who lives in Hebei – who are relatively wealthy but have few women around them."Our clients are free to choose whoever they like. The purpose of our business is to help people find someone they genuinely want to be with."One of the advertisements assures their prospective clients that "Three days with the right introduction can beat three years of dating".Image caption, It was in a room like this where Wang met his brideWang now spends his time trying to help other victims of similar spiels.His rented flat is full of men who are either searching for the owners of the agency who scammed them, or are trying to recoup their losses from their wives who ran off after only a few weeks of marriage.On a fold-up bed by the window, 59-year-old Xu Rulin from Jiangxi province pulls his carefully collated evidence out of a red plastic shopping bag.He spent nearly 500,000 yuan trying to find his son a wife through a "flash marriage" agency.Together they travelled to Guiyang - more than 1,000km away - and his son wed just seven days after he first met his bride in a "blind date" room.Xu says after the marriage was registered, she demanded they buy her an iPhone and transfer around 20,000 yuan to help her with her business. She also asked for 120,000 yuan for a wedding dress and jewellery, he claims."All I wanted was for her to genuinely settle down and live with us," he told us. "She said she wanted a house and I agreed to buy one for them. It was all agreed."But he says she ran away after living with them for less than two weeks. She has been detained by the police, and the couple have been able to get divorced.He says the owners of the matchmaking company were also arrested in January this year, but he is still in Guiyang trying to recover some of the losses.Image caption, The bride Xu Rulin spent a fortune finding for his son ran away within two weeksThe agency manager the BBC spoke to admitted there were no formal background checks on their clients."The women are introduced by local matchmakers who already know them very well. They know their family background because they're often from the same village. The male's matchmaker also usually knows the man very well."They would not say how much their services cost because that information was "confidential".He did say that if the information provided by either side is not truthful, then the client is entitled to get their money back."I'd say more than 90% of what our clients tell us here is true," he claimed."We have a saying here in China. One rotten mouse dropping spoils the whole pot of soup. That's exactly what it's like. We regularly attend meetings with the local police. If a matchmaking agency is found to be involved in marriage fraud, it will be held legally responsible."Image caption, This matchmaker says most people in the industry are genuineThis brings little comfort for those who have lost whatever money they had saved."I never imagined that with the agency charging such a high service fee, a local matchmaker in her hometown checking her background and the company offering so many guarantees, that the women's information would turn out to be completely fake," Wang says.He is almost resigned now to his losses. And he blames himself for falling for the scam: "Only women with problems would agree to these kind of flash marriages."He has kneeled at the police offices in Guiyang pleading for them to help him get his money back and he has even travelled to Beijing to urge the authorities to do more to combat this type of crime.These cases are difficult to prosecute, says Fan Binghe, the lawyer who has handled many.For one, Chinese law has no specific criminal offence which covers this kind of marriage fraud, and so to bring criminal charges, a victim has to establish that the aim of their spouse was always to take their money."In cases I've handled, suspects often argue that they genuinely intended to marry and live a good life but realised they were incompatible, had conflicts, and decided to end the relationship," he says."In situations like that, the line becomes blurred. Relationship issues are difficult to disprove."Image caption, Wang's apartment has turned into a refuge for scammed menEven harder is getting money back from sham matchmaking agencies which often shut up shop as soon as they have made enough cash.Wang has managed to get some money back, but not all."After going through something like this, I don't even know if I can still get married. It was already hard for me to find someone. And now I've spent so much money. I won't consider it now."Wang's life, and the life of the men in the apartment, all appear to be in limbo."It has taken almost two years, and even now I still don't know when I can divorce her," he says, surrounded by his legal paperwork."I don't know when this will be resolved, so I can restart a normal life. It feels endless."

schema.headline: The lonely Chinese men being conned by fake brides

title: Schools with more disadvantaged children missing swimming target
description: Swimming lessons 'vital' as schools gap revealedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Primary schools across England are expected to teach key swim
body: Swimming lessons 'vital' as schools gap revealedImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Primary schools across England are expected to teach key swimming skills to keep children safe in waterByLauren Woodhead and Ema SabljakEngland Data UnitChildren at English primary schools with more pupils on free school meals are less likely to leave able to swim 25m, BBC research has found.While 72% of Year 6 children on average left school able to swim 25m in 2024-25, this drops to just 55% for schools with a higher proportion of disadvantaged children.Ashley Jones, head of water safety and education at the Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS), said it was "absolutely vital" children were equipped with basic swimming and self-rescue skills.A Department for Education (DfE) spokesperson said it was aware of the gap and it "needs to change".The national curriculum in England, external states when they leave Year 6, all pupils should be able to:Swim competently, confidently and proficiently over a distance of at least 25mUse a range of strokes effectively (for example, front crawl, backstroke and breaststroke)Perform safe self-rescue in different water-based situationsA BBC Freedom of Information request to the DfE has revealed the proportion of Year 6 pupils at individual state schools, excluding special schools, who are able to meet the targets. While 70% of 2024-25 Year 6 leavers nationally could on average perform a safe self-rescue, only half of children from schools with the highest level of free meal eligibility could do so.A safe self-rescue includes being able to tread water for 30 seconds, children being able to float on their back for 60 seconds and swim 15m to exit the water unaided.Most school groups only get six weeks of 30-minute sessions to learn basic swimming skills – three hours in total.The findings come after several water-related deaths this summer, including an 18-year-old man who died after getting into difficulty at sea at the weekend in East Sussex.Find out how your child's school performedSchool performance ranged from no pupils leaving Year 6 able to swim 25m to others meeting the target at 100%. Only 38 schools in the highest category for disadvantaged pupils hit the swimming target. Meanwhile, it was met by nearly 400 schools with the lowest proportion of children on free school meals.For parents, there can be several obstacles when it comes to helping their children learn to swim and become water competent.In 2021, Swim England published its Decade of Decline report, external warning almost 2,000 swimming pools could be lost forever by 2030.Accessibility is one of the factors Ashley Jones from the RLSS says limits children's swimming education."We've got some incredible public leisure facilities, just not enough of them," he said."That means people have got to travel further. "Then you are dependent on public transport, which can be costly, and access to a swimming pool in terms of cost and time is still really challenging."Some schools are tackling transport costs in innovative ways, such as in Derby where a pop-up swimming pool was set up on school grounds.Image source, RLSS UKImage caption, Ashley Jones says swimming lessons should be "universal, engaging and accessible"The RLSS works to help people stay safe in, on, and around water. A key element of its work is using education to help people become water competent.Jones explained: "You can be a really competent pool swimmer, but we wouldn't dare put you in 6ft of surf or throw you in a raging river."Building competence, you've got to have knowledge, you've got to have skills, you've got to have experience, crucially, and you've got to have training."In order to help children build water competency, Jones believes swimming lessons need to be universal, engaging and accessible.The RLSS would like to see "a fully funded, fully supported, high-level learn to swim programme" that is supported by water safety education and then applied in an outdoor environment.Hampshire-based swimming teacher Bethany Harris said it was "really tough" to teach a life skill in that time to children who have not had much access to swimming.She believes school swimming lessons should start earlier in life to ensure nobody is left behind."Ultimately, in three hours you can't take someone from being a nervous swimmer to confidently being able to swim 25m with a stroke that is calm and is going to keep them safe," she said."I don't think many of us would come out of that with something that was going to save our lives potentially."I think it needs to come in basically as we're teaching them to read and write in the infant school."Harris lives "on the doorstep" of Hawley Lake, near Farnborough, where a 14-year-old died in May after going missing while swimming."Even being inland away from the coast you've got dangerous water all about," she said.The bottom fifth of local authorities for the average proportion of children able to swim 25m were all urban areas.Only four out of 31 of those council areas were coastal, with the remaining areas being landlocked.Overall, fewer children in urban areas could swim the distance proficiently than in rural areas.Harris would also like to see pools offer more initiatives to ensure they are accessible to all families.She said: "Ten years ago, there used to be a summer scheme where you could swim for £1 all summer long through some leisure centres."I haven't heard of anything like that happening locally these days."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Fewer than two-thirds of Year 6 children at primary schools in urban areas could perform a self-rescueA spokesperson for the DfE said a new PE Partnership Network would help close the gap seen by disadvantaged children.It will bring together schools, local clubs and national bodies like Swim England."This means targeted support for the areas and pupils who need it most, so that every child, wherever they live, gets the same chance to learn to swim," the spokesperson said.Swim England is working closely with the government to support the delivery of school swimming lessons."Swimming is a life skill, not just a sport, and every child should have the opportunity to leave primary school able to swim and be safe in, on and around water," a spokesperson said."However, schools have faced significant pressures in recent years, particularly those serving disadvantaged communities, including competing curriculum demands, increasing transport costs and access to suitable swimming pools."These challenges are real, so it is more important than ever that there is a collective approach to helping children gain a skill that could one day save their life."Additional reporting by Jonathan Fagg and Emily UniaFigure caption, Welcome to Brown Gal Can't Swim

title: The Cambridge University lecturer who kept her Tourette's secret
description: 'I felt Tourette's would ruin my life, now I teach at Cambridge'Image caption, Throughout her academic life, Dr Amanda Cole has kept her Tourette's hi
body: 'I felt Tourette's would ruin my life, now I teach at Cambridge'Image caption, Throughout her academic life, Dr Amanda Cole has kept her Tourette's hidden - until nowByLaurence CawleyEast InvestigationsDr Amanda Cole was 15 and sitting in a religious studies class when she experienced a peculiar spasm at the back of throat. She assumed it would pass, but it was a vocal tic and her first known manifestation of her Tourette's syndrome, a condition that causes people to make sudden, repetitive sounds or movements."How am I going to have a family? How am I going to have a job?" Cole, 32, remembers asking herself as she lay awake at night after her diagnosis in her 20s at her home on the Debden Estate near the London-Essex border. "I thought it was going to destroy my life."Now a married mother-of-one, Cole is an assistant professor in sociolinguistics at Cambridge University, but throughout her academic life she has kept her Tourette's hidden - until now.Following an incident at this year's Bafta Film Awards ceremony in which a guest shouted out offensive words because of his tics, Cole said she wanted to be open about her condition and allowed the BBC to join her as she began telling colleagues and students.Image source, Cole familyImage caption, When growing up, Cole did not tell friends or classmates about her Tourette's"I felt so scared of Tourette's," says Cole, who is one of about 300,000 people in the UK living with the condition. "There was no-one I knew that had Tourette's, and I didn't see anyone in the public eye that had Tourette's - and if they did, they were a figure of ridicule. "The only impression I had of Tourette's was people acting... and they were swearing, and they were shouting, and they were being obnoxious."As a result, she hid the condition from friends growing up and colleagues by either by suppressing the tics or releasing them when the person she was speaking with looked away.Even now, Cole says she retains "some residual shame" about her condition and wants to live in a world where people can "tic freely" without embarrassment. "It's quite liberating telling people, whether it's students or friends because most of the time people are just like 'oh, OK, fine'," says Cole, who is also autistic.The most recent data from the Higher Education Statistics Agency, external shows out of about 245,000 academic staff working in the UK's institutions, just 70 - or 0.03% - have disclosed a developmental condition that affects motor or cognitive skills.Experts believe the true number may be far highe, externalr and that many academics with conditions such as Tourette's hide their neurodiversity for fear of repercussions.Cole's vocal tics tend to include the names of her husband, her son or the family cat or random phrases such as "good night" during the day time."I worry a little bit [that] I'm like the palatable face of Tourette's  - I don't swear, I don't say anything that is going to be too challenging."I think what we just really need as society is an understanding of Tourette's, an understanding of tics and to know that tics aren't what we really think," she says.The words are merely "a neurological event that we have no control over", she adds.Emma McNally, the chief executive at Tourette's Action, says many of those with coprolalia end up self-isolating from society.She adds that many people with Tourette's find people accepting of their condition until they say something that feels as though "it's about them"."People then take offence even though there's no malice behind it," says McNally. While Cole and many others with Tourette's have developed often very sophisticated strategies to mask their tics, not everybody can suppress them, McNally says.But unreleased tics need to come out at some point, Cole says, and storing them up is physically uncomfortable - she describes the sensation as akin to an "itch" or "suppressing a sneeze". When she is alone, she will then spend time releasing all of those suppressed tics - a process that can take a few minutes."I've gone to great lengths at times to hide my Tourette's," she says. "Some people with Tourette's can't suppress at all, and some people can suppress to a lesser or greater degree."Women, she says, tend to be more adept at "masking" the condition.Image caption, After giving a morning lecture about accents, Cole joined students Tim Morrice (left) and Abbie Lovewell for a supervision sessionThe BBC joined Cole in May for her first lecture in which every student was aware of her Tourette's."I had no idea until she told us," says linguistic student Tim Morrice. "But I really appreciate her telling us because I think it's really nice to see neurodivergent people in academia because it isn't a thing we see or hear very much."Fellow student Abbie Lovewell says finding out about Cole's Tourette's made absolutely "no difference" to her or how she views her supervisor."I think she's one of the best supervisors that I've had," she adds. 'Productive superpowers'When asked if she would take a magic pill that removed her Tourette's, Cole responds with a firm "no"."I wouldn't ever want to get rid of my Tourette's because my brain is wired the way my brain is wired, and I like being me and the people that love me, like me being me."Tourette's, she says, can also offer a selection of "superpowers"."I really have hyperfocus - something that has been well-documented as part of Tourette's," she says, describing being able to spend hours on a task she has set herself such as research, painting or playing the piano. "I can really, really focus and be really, really, really productive," she says.Image caption, Cole's husband, Ed Wellington, says he did not realise his wife had Tourette's at firstHowever, there can be disadvantages to Cole's hyperfocus, according to her husband Ed Wellington, such as getting her attention when she is involved in a task or her refusal to stop doing household tasks in spite of the time, once she has begun.Her tics and her Tourette's in general, however, have never been something the pair have really discussed, he says."From when I first met her, I could sort of tell she had something about her - she had real energy and drive," says Wellington. "I didn't know she had Tourette's. I didn't know that for quite some time."He describes making various small adjustments to prevent Cole being "overwhelmed" by sensory stimuli, such as leaving the room to eat crisps because the crunching sound feels like it is coming through a "megaphone right into her ear"."If she's feeling really over-stimulated I have to like go around like turning off all the main lights," he says. "I have to Tourette-proof the room for her a bit."Figure caption, Why I decided to stop hiding my Tourette’sOwing to Tourette's often being genetic, Cole says if her son develops the condition she will encourage to him to "harness" its "huge strengths". "I know any mother is going to say this, but he is going to be wonderful because he is already wonderful." When asked what she would say to her frightened 15-year-old self, Cole says: "You're going to be fine, you don't need to be scared, Tourette's is fine."I don't feel I've lived my life despite my Tourette's, I feel I've lived my life well with Tourette's and autism. It has really helped me achieve and made me the person I am."I think my teenage self would be well happy if she could see me now." title: Skegness visitors going home earlier, seaside traders say
description: Image caption, Craig Watts, who runs the Boating Lake Cafe, thinks people do not have money to spend on luxuriesByJessica Lanein SkegnessSeaside trade
body: Image caption, Craig Watts, who runs the Boating Lake Cafe, thinks people do not have money to spend on luxuriesByJessica Lanein SkegnessSeaside traders believe people are spending fewer evenings and less cash in one of the biggest resorts on England's east coast.Restaurateurs, publicans and shop owners in Skegness, Lincolnshire, say business is down significantly this summer.Statistics gathered for East Lindsey District Council show that there were 2.94 million visitors to the coast in 2025, 8% higher than in 2024, with an economic impact of almost £752m (up 15%).But Craig Watts, who runs a fish and chip cafe by the seafront, says: "We've had all this great weather this year. People are coming, but there's no money."He adds: "We're struggling to stay open until 5.30pm now and we're not opening as early as we used to.  "We see an arrival at around 12 noon and at 4pm it's dropping off. It's day trippers."Image caption, Hilary Fox says visitors are not spending as much money this yearHilary Fox, who has owned the factory rock shop on the main shopping street for 57 years, echoes his views."We close around 7.30pm now. We used to be here until nine, but there's nobody about," she says. "I think there's more day trippers than holidaymakers, so they want to get home."There's lots of people about in the day. It's just not the same. I don't think they've got the money."Image caption, Richard Underwood says his pub has not seen enough good days this yearAt the Suncastle pub, landlord Richard Underwood says the summer is vital to tourist resorts."We rely on a huge influx of visitors during the school holidays and footfall is definitely down."It's been a very strange season so far. We've had some really busy days, but not enough. It has been a struggle at times."The venue, which opened in 1932 as a tea room and solarium, has been in Underwood's family since 2004. But he has had to cut back evening entertainment from every night to weekends only."Evenings are not what we've been used to. I'd say it's a gradual trend we've seen over the last two or three years," he says. "People haven't got the resources to sit in a pub for three or four hours and enjoy themselves. I get the impression people are holidaying on a tighter budget."'More than ever'East Lindsey District Council says official visitor figures for 2026 are not available yet, but 2025 was a good year.Speaking in July, councillor Steve Kirk, the portfolio holder for the coastal economy, said statistics showed "more people than ever" were "choosing to stay and enjoy everything our coastal communities have to offer".Across the whole district, which also includes the popular Lincolnshire Wolds, there were 1.927 million staying visitors (up 13% on 2024) and 2.837 million day visitors (up 2.7%).They supported 6,814 jobs across the district, up 5%.However, the figures did show a shift in where people stay, with the number of visitor days for serviced accommodation in East Lindsey falling from 856,000 in 2023 to 722,000 in 2025.During the same period, visitor days in non-serviced accommodation rose from 8.1 million to 8.9 million.Image caption, Aiobheann Collins-Gould and her family save up for their holiday to Skegness each yearVisitors to Skegness say they still love their holidays, but are doing their best to cut back on spending.Aiobheann Collins-Gould comes to the resort every year with her family from Birmingham. They save up so they can get away, but she says it is still hard to afford."If you have younger kids you're up early and out of the house, so you're spending money from seven in the morning, so you can't really stay out until seven in the evening – especially with the price of everything going up."Lerato Marumo, from Nottingham, is on holiday with her two children. "It's not as busy as we thought it would be here, but there's still a lot to do. I will go broke by the end of the week," she says. Image caption, Rachel Garriock, with her mother Mary and daughter. They say they go back to their accommodation in the eveningsRachel Garriock, from Nottingham, is on holiday with her mother and daughter. She says it feels busier than in previous years, but adds: "We don't go out at night because we've got the little one. "It was quiet before we went home yesterday – it had definitely quietened down by about 7pm."One issue identified by Skegness Town Council involves street lights being turned off at midnight in some parts of town as a cost-saving measure, meaning some residents and holidaymakers have to walk to their homes or caravan parks in darkness. Taxpayers have been asked if they are prepared to pay extra to turn them back on.Watts, whose family has run the Boating Lake Cafe for about 27 years, fears that if current trends continue, the resort will suffer. "We realistically have 10 trading weeks to make money. You work towards the school holidays. "We're doing different offers now. A mini fish and chips which is cheaper, which we've not done previously [and] Monday to Friday ice cream offers. We're trying to regain some money back, but it's difficult."Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.Get in touchYour Voice

title: My brother was found dead – but police didn't realise for days that he had been shot
description: Image source, Douglas LowImage caption, Brian Low was murdered on a rural path near Aberfeldy in February 2024ByGraeme OgstonTayside and Central repor
body: Image source, Douglas LowImage caption, Brian Low was murdered on a rural path near Aberfeldy in February 2024ByGraeme OgstonTayside and Central reporterUpdated 7 hours agoBrian Low was walking his dog on a remote country path when he was shot dead by a former colleague whose hatred had festered for years.The 65-year-old was found near Aberfeldy in Highland Perthshire with blood on his hands and face - but police did not realise at first that he had been murdered.The former groundsman's death was not treated as suspicious for several days, until a post-mortem examination confirmed he had died from gunshot wounds. Shotgun pellets had fallen from the body bag before his body was examined.It was another three months before the killer, retired gamekeeper David Campbell, was arrested.He is now serving life for murder - but Brian Low's family still cannot understand the mistakes which were made after his body was found.They have spoken publicly for the first time in two-part BBC documentary Murder Trial: Death of a Dog Walker, which follows the police investigation and the trial."I was so angry and so sad at the same time," says his brother Douglas Low."How could this happen?"Image source, Firecrest MediaImage caption, Brian Low's brother Douglas said he was angry and sad at the police blunderBrian Low's body was discovered on Leafy Lane, with his dog Millie by his side, on the morning of 17 February 2024.One of the first detectives on the scene told the murder trial that he believed Low's injuries were consistent with him falling while out for a walk.The court was shown graphic photographs of Low's body lying on the path. His face was covered in blood and black marks.Douglas Low said the pictures were "so horrific I barely kept my breakfast down. I can't imagine why someone would say that's a medical event".Brian's niece, Jacqui Low, added: "It just seems incredible that they didn't see the marks on his face, the shot."The post-mortem found that Low's clothes were peppered with holes and he had sustained about 30 pellet injuries.Figure caption, Pam Curran: Everybody liked Brian, he didn’t have a bad bone in his bodyThe delays meant that a cordon at the crime scene was not put in place until 23 February, six days after Low's body was found.Det Ch Insp Martin MacDougall, of the Major Investigation Team, said: "When you have that delay, a number of things go through your mind of what we could potentially have lost evidentially."Footprints in the soil, tyre tracks, CCTV."The murder inquiry was finally launched 10 days after Low's body was discovered.A press conference took place a few days later, where MacDougall and colleague Ch Insp Greg Burns were grilled over the blunder.One detective told the filmmakers that there had been a lot of media interest and admitted: "We're kind of a wee bit on the back foot".Murder Trial: Death of a Dog WalkerBrian Low is shot and found dead in rural Scotland. David Campbell, former gamekeeper of the shooting estate where he worked, stands accused of his premeditated murder.Over the next three months police spoke to 800 witnesses and trawled through 2,400 hours of CCTV footage from 56 cameras.The documentary followed prosecutor Greg Farrell as his team built the case against Campbell, as well as the accused's lawyer, Tony Lenehan KC, as he attempted to dismantle the prosecution's timeline and cast doubt on the evidence.Because of the potential missed forensic opportunities, the prosecution led a circumstantial case during the trial.It linked smaller strands of evidence to build a picture of Campbell's decades-old grudge against Low, who had worked at the nearby Edradynate Estate with his future killer for more than 20 years.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, David Campbell was jailed for a minimum of 19 years for murdering Brian LowCampbell had been the head gamekeeper at the estate.He was described by local farmer Sally Crystal as "highly respected" and a man who "ran a very, very good shoot".Crystal had first met Campbell during the 1987 shooting season.She said that when he first arrived he had been an excellent gamekeeper - but as his reputation grew, he became "very arrogant"."David started really misbehaving, the family (who ran Edradynate) started mistrusting him," said Crystal.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, Sally Crystal told the trial that David Campbell told her he "hated" Brian LowAsked during the trial how the two men got along, she said: "At first it wasn't noticeable, but as time went on there was a coldness."On at least one occasion I had been talking to Brian in the morning and David walked past me."He turned to me, angry because I was slightly late that morning and I'd still had time to talk to Brian."He walked away and he said I (expletive) loathe that man. I hate him."Image caption, A police cordon was not erected at the scene until days after Brian Low's deathPam Curran, who was Low's partner for 22 years, said everyone who met Brian liked him."I don't think he had a bad bone in his body," she said.Douglas Low said he had not thought that his brother had an enemy in the world."Who would want to harm Brian? He was the nicest, kindest person you could ever imagine," he said."It's just so unbelievable."However, the trial was told of bad blood between the two men.Campbell had suspected Low of "planting" items which were allegedly found during a raid on his then-home on the estate after alleged bird poisonings.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, The documentary includes footage of Campbell's arrest three months after the murderCampbell said he had not had any contact with Low since 2017 and that he did not know he had left Edradynate Estate until he saw it on television.Pam Curran said: "I knew they had a fall-out, a serious one because Dave was being investigated for poisoning birds of prey and it had happened more than once."And whatever Brian had said to the police really angered Dave and they had a right set-to."Brian wouldn't tell me the ins and outs of it, but I knew it was bad. Brian was really upset by it."Campbell was removed from Edradynate in early 2017 having worked there for more than 30 years.During the trial, defence advocate Lenehan noted that in the seven years since he had left the estate both men had lived near each other without there being any issue.But in reality, Campbell had been planning how to kill Low - and cover his tracks.Figure caption, Watch: David Campbell covers doorbell with duct tapeOn the morning of Friday 16 February 2024, Campbell set to work on his plan.He covered the CCTV camera at the rear of his home with duct tape in the morning, not removing it until that evening.A figure the prosecution said was Campbell was seen on CCTV riding through Aberfeldy on a distinctive bicycle, heading in the direction of the murder scene.One witness told the trial that Campbell had later asked a bike repair shop to change the tyres.The police also saw CCTV footage from a nearby farm showing a "spooked " horse running around a field, at the same time Low was believed to have been shot.Officers say the time matched the last known activity from Low's mobile phone.Image source, Firecrest FilmsImage caption, CCTV showed a horse in a nearby field that was "spooked" at the same time police believe Brian Low was shotThree months after the killing, police finally arrested Campbell.He was on the toilet naked when officers arrived at his home.In a combative police interview, Campbell was asked by arresting officer Det Con David Budd if Low's death had been an accident."I don't know," he replied.Budd asked him: "Well did you mean to shoot him or not?" - to which Campbell replied: "Cheeky bastard."He went on to say that he "100%" did not have anything to do with Brian Low's death.Image source, Firecrest MoviesImage caption, David Campbell's combative police interview is shown in the documentaryCampbell gave evidence in his own defence during the trial.He said he spent most of the day in his house and made a lengthy call to the local council about a planning application.Campbell said he did not ask for a solicitor after his arrest because he "didn't need one" and denied having anything to do with Low's death.However, he was found guilty of murder after a 15-day trial at the High Court in Glasgow. The jury delivered its verdict after three days of deliberations.Judge Lord Scott told Campbell his "targeted assassination" had been "an appalling and senseless act of extreme wickedness."He was jailed for life and ordered to serve a minimum of 19 years before he can apply for parole.Figure caption, Judge Lord Scott: 'You believed you had got away with murder'Pam Curran said she had not been able to go into court for the verdict because she did not know how she would react."That one act of violence has changed so many people's lives, and for what?"An argument over something on an estate that happened years ago."She said her life would never be the same."I'm not getting to see Brian ever again. How is that right?""But you can't feel sorry for yourself."You just have to pick yourself up and keep going, because that's what he would have wanted."

schema.headline: My brother was found dead – but police didn't realise for days that he had been shot

title: Call with No 10 has given us hope, PC Andrew Harper's mother says
description: Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, they will become eligible for
body: Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020. Under changes to the Sentencing Act made this year, they will become eligible for release from custody next January.They are in a category of prisoners - those who have committed certain serious violent or sexual crimes - who until now would have had to serve at least two-thirds of their sentence in jail before being considered for release.Downing Street had earlier warned it would not be possible to exclude "one or two offenders" convicted of manslaughter from the early release scheme.However, the BBC has been told that Burnham has now instructed his justice secretary to find a way to exclude Cole and Bowers from the scheme designed to ease prison overcrowding.In a later statement, the PM said he was "increasingly confident" that work to increase space in the prison system "will allow us to reduce the number of people released early".He added: "And, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC [Andrew] Harper, prevent their early release altogether."Adlam said the conflicting reports had been making her "more and more angry" and the uncertainty had left her family "in turmoil".Of the phone call she received, she said. "I think the fact it's actually come from Downing Street, I've got to try and have some faith in it, but at the same time I've got to protect my own feelings."Thames Valley Police officer PC Harper, 28, from Wallingford, Oxfordshire, died in 2019 when he was dragged behind the getaway car of three teenagers who had fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.Adlam said: "Everybody is watching this. This is obviously extremely personal to us but it's to do with the country as a whole really. This is really vital to get right, it feels like a hash, like a rush job."Speaking about Cole and Bowers, she added: "They weren't given extreme sentences and I'm only asking for them to do what they were given, I'm not asking for anything more than they were sentenced."Aileen O'Connor, chairman of Thames Valley Police Federation, said the reports that Burnham would look to exclude Cole and Bowers from the early release scheme, gave her a "little glimmer of hope".She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Police officers up and down this country run towards danger, they put themselves on the line every single day and Andrew Harper paid the ultimate sacrifice for the job that he loved and the badge he wore."We need to see the government protecting us because we're getting battered all over the show every single day."Housing, Communities and Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner said the government was still looking at all options around the prisons crisis and preventing the early release of PC Harper's killers.She told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday: "The trauma that PC Harper's family has been through, and other victims who are watching this crisis unfold in our prisons, is unacceptable."The prime minister has said that those serious offenders, like the ones that killed PC Harper, he doesn't want to see them released early and he has tasked the justice secretary to look at that and to come to parliament in September so that we can do everything we possibly can to stop that from happening."Last week, PC Harper's widow, Lissie Harper, said she "will not give up" and hoped people would share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison.She said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets."Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."More than 900,000 people have signed the petition set up by Thames Valley Police Federation, which calls the decision for Cole and Bowers to be eligible for early release an "insult".

schema.headline: Call with No 10 has given us hope, PC Andrew Harper's mother says

title: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift
description: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaic
body: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult.During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good".That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue.Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands.While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson.""She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded.The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia."The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday.Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188)."So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China.An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question".He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights."Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology.Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments.Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting".Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said". "I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven.Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan.The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above".Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments".Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

schema.headline: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift

title: Murder arrest over fatal shooting in Clapham
description: A man has died in a shooting in south London and police have arrested a suspect on suspicion of murder.Officers and paramedics were called to Willingt
body: A man has died in a shooting in south London and police have arrested a suspect on suspicion of murder.Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor Pub.A 25-year-old man was found injured and was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.Shortly after the shooting, a 22-year-old man attended hospital with a gunshot wound. He was arrested and remains in hospital while police await an update on his condition, the force added.Det Ch Supt Emma Bond, central south borough commander, said: "We understand that this incident will cause concern within the local community and an increased police presence will remain in the area throughout the day as our inquiries continue. "Our thoughts remain with the victim's family for their tragic loss."Police are asking anyone with any further information that could help the investigation to come forward.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external.
